name: Christianity
summary: A family of traditions centered on the life and teaching of Jesus of Nazareth, read through scripture and centuries of theological reflection. Moral life is framed as a response to divine love: love of God and neighbor ground the commandments, and conscience is formed within a community seeking holiness.

key_concepts.gloss: self-giving love of God and neighbor, the measure of the law
every person bears the image of God and so has inviolable worth
moral failure is real but met by forgiveness and transformation
in Catholic thought, moral order knowable by reason (Aquinas)

name: Islam
summary: Submission to God as revealed in the Qur'an and modeled by the Prophet Muhammad. Ethics is guided by divine command interpreted through jurisprudence, ordering acts from obligatory to forbidden, with mercy, justice, and accountability before God as constant themes.

key_concepts.gloss: God-consciousness; mindfulness that one acts before God
the permitted and the forbidden in the five-fold ranking of acts
obligatory almsgiving as purification of wealth
patient steadfastness under trial

name: Judaism
era: Biblical era onward; rabbinic period c. 70–500 CE
summary: Covenantal life with God expressed in commandments and refined through rabbinic argument. The Torah's obligations are interpreted case by case in the Talmud and codes; ethical seriousness shows in the tradition's willingness to weigh duty against duty in concrete situations.

key_concepts.gloss: a commandment; the unit of obligation in covenantal life
saving a life overrides nearly every other commandment
righteousness enacted as obligatory giving
the evil tongue; derogatory speech even when true

name: Buddhism
summary: A path out of suffering taught by the Buddha: conduct, meditation, and wisdom support one another. Ethics begins in intention — actions rooted in greed, hatred, or delusion bind, while those rooted in generosity, kindness, and clear seeing free — and non-harm extends to all sentient beings.

key_concepts.gloss: non-harm toward all sentient beings
intentional action shaping future experience
loving-kindness cultivated toward all beings
undertakings against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants

name: Hinduism
summary: A vast family of traditions ordered around dharma — the duty proper to one's station, stage of life, and situation — and the pursuit of liberation. Texts from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita weigh ritual duty, non-attachment, and non-harm, often insisting that the same act differs morally with role and intent.

key_concepts.gloss: duty and right order, indexed to role and circumstance
non-injury, praised as the highest dharma
acting without attachment to the fruits of action
liberation, the final aim beyond merit

name: Confucianism
summary: A Chinese ethical tradition centered on the cultivation of character within relationships — family, community, state. Moral life is learned through ritual propriety and the practice of humaneness rather than derived from abstract rules.

key_concepts.gloss: humaneness; the cardinal virtue of benevolent regard for others
ritual propriety; the forms through which respect is enacted
trustworthiness in word and deed
reciprocity: do not impose on others what you would not wish for yourself

name: Stoicism
summary: A Greco-Roman school teaching that virtue is the only true good and that a good life is lived in agreement with nature and reason. What lies outside the will — reputation, wealth, even death — is indifferent; the work of ethics is mastering judgment, desire, and response.

key_concepts.gloss: the faculty of choice; the only thing wholly our own
freedom from destructive passion, not from feeling
widening circles of concern from self to all rational beings
some things are in our power, others are not

name: Kantian deontology
summary: Immanuel Kant's moral philosophy grounds duty in reason itself: act only on maxims you could will as universal law, and treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Moral worth lies in acting from duty, and persons possess a dignity beyond all price.

key_concepts.gloss: the unconditional command of morality, testable by universalization
never treat rational nature merely as a means
self-legislation by practical reason
worth beyond price, admitting no trade-offs

name: Utilitarianism
summary: The tradition of Bentham, Mill, and Sidgwick: actions and institutions are right insofar as they promote the greatest happiness, with each person's welfare counting equally. Its reforming edge comes from asking of every rule and custom what suffering it prevents or produces.

key_concepts.gloss: right action maximizes happiness, impartially counted
everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one
assess single acts directly, or the rules whose adoption does best
the capacity to suffer as the boundary of moral concern

name: Virtue ethics
summary: Anchored in Aristotle: the moral question is not first about acts or rules but about character — what habits and traits constitute a flourishing human life. Virtue lies in a mean discovered by practical wisdom, and is learned by practice within a community.

key_concepts.gloss: flourishing; the final end of human life
practical wisdom that discerns the right act in the particular case
virtue as an intermediate between excess and deficiency
character formed by repeated action
